book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook starts with BIS and the Basel Committee, lists Basel I-III with dates, and then defines capital adequacy. Here the video starts with the danger: running a bank is risky, a failed bank cannot repay depositors, and one failure spreads to all banks, to industry and to the whole world. The Basel norms come in as the protection (keep money aside, like spare cash in an inner pocket on a bus), then the institutions behind them, and only then each risk is taken apart, credit risk as a full story. The format is overview first, details after, with a sidebar map that lights the current risk; the capital ratios are named but left for later.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Overview then details: first show the whole problem and its fix in one panel, then return to each piece (institution, each risk) one at a time, ticking it on a sidebar map.

opening.what: Says the video starts with an overview and then covers each topic in detail; an OVERVIEW chip, a bank with the Basel accords and three chips, and CAR, CRAR, RWA with their full names appear.

moves.concept: three bank risks (overview)
moves.what: Overview first, then each topic in detail.

moves.concept: three bank risks (overview)
moves.what: Running a bank is not easy; its risks fall into three types (credit, market, operational), any of which can make it fail.

moves.concept: bank failure and its chain of effects
moves.what: 'Bank fail hone ka matlab aap samajhte ho?' Depositors will not get back the money they kept with the bank.

moves.concept: bank failure and its chain of effects
moves.what: 'Soch ke dekho': people lose trust, the financial system becomes unstable, people pull money from all banks, banks cannot lend to industry, the economy cannot grow; yaani one bank's failure can cause a downturn.

moves.concept: bank failure and its chain of effects
moves.what: Would one country's downturn affect the world economy? 'Padega, bilkul padega.'

moves.concept: Basel norms: keep money aside against risk
moves.what: To prevent this, BIS issued the Basel norms, also called accords (Basel 1, 2, 3), which ask banks to keep some money aside to cover these risks.

moves.concept: Basel norms: keep money aside against risk
moves.what: Like travelling on a state bus and fearing pickpockets, you keep some cash in an inner pocket so that you can still get home.

moves.concept: Basel norms: keep money aside against risk
moves.what: How does a bank decide how much money is enough? Promises CAR, CRAR, RWA and tier 1 and tier 2 capital 'in this video' (they are not covered in it).

moves.concept: BIS: what it is, who owns it, what it does
moves.what: Before all that, what is BIS and what does it do?

moves.concept: BIS: what it is, who owns it, what it does
moves.what: The world's oldest international financial institution, set up in 1930 at Basel, Switzerland, owned by 62 central banks covering about 95% of world GDP.

moves.concept: BIS: what it is, who owns it, what it does
moves.what: Central banks cooperate and exchange information through BIS, and so it promotes monetary and financial stability; it also gives banking services to central banks.

moves.concept: BCBS develops the Basel norms
moves.what: Among BIS committees, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (1974, G10 central bank governors, later enlarged) developed the norms that keep global banking sound and stable: the Basel norms.

moves.concept: BCBS develops the Basel norms
moves.what: So far: what BIS is and what it does.

moves.concept: credit risk
moves.what: Before Basel 1, 2, 3 we must understand the risks banks face.

moves.concept: credit risk
moves.what: Interest on loans is a bank's income, so more loans means more income; but there is no guarantee a loan comes back, so more loans means more risk.

moves.concept: credit risk
moves.what: The lent money is not the bank's own: it is depositors' money (plus equity and market borrowing); if loans are not recovered the bank cannot repay depositors, and 'taala lagna tay hai'.

moves.concept: credit risk
moves.what: The word for a loan or 'udhaar' is credit, so this risk is credit risk.

moves.concept: market risk
moves.what: Banks invest surplus funds in gold, securities, bonds, shares, real estate; some swing in price fast, and that is market risk.

moves.concept: operational risk
moves.what: Banks also face operational risk: fraud, robbery ('dakaiti'), cyber attacks, server failure or data loss.

moves.concept: Basel I, II, III and how central banks apply them
moves.what: To mitigate these, BCBS formulated Basel 1 (screen shows 1988; the transcript reads 1998), Basel 2 in 2004, and Basel 3 in 2010, which banks follow now.

moves.concept: Basel I, II, III and how central banks apply them
moves.what: The norms are guidelines for each member's central bank, which may apply them as they are or modified (the RBI column on screen).

moves.concept: Basel I, II, III and how central banks apply them
moves.what: That is all for today; next video covers Basel 1, 2 and 3 in detail.

closing.what: Stops after the Basel timeline and the RBI column (rules flow from BCBS through RBI to the bank) and points to the next video for Basel 1-3; a promo banner covers part of the summary; CAR, CRAR, RWA and tier capital are left unexplained.

narration.density: About 26 terms (credit, market and operational risk, depositors, financial instability, contagion, credit crunch, economic downturn, BIS, Basel norms, Basel accords, Basel I/II/III, CAR, CRAR, RWA, tier 1 and tier 2 capital, international financial institution, BCBS, G10, equity, debt, surplus funds, fraud, cyber attack) in about 410 s, about 4 per minute. The overview (80-146 s) names about 10 terms in a minute, several of which the video never explains; the details half is comfortable.

talmel_summary: In the overview and the BIS facts the picture mostly writes what is said (bullets, fact lines, abbreviation lines), sometimes 2 s early. The details half shows the step well: an interest loop that is later crossed out, 'more loan, more income, more risk' tags, deposits flowing in, a FAIL seal, and a long dotted curve filing the story under 'credit risk' on the sidebar map; BIS as a hub and the committee as a table with heads are good small pictures. The best spoken idea (the bus inner-pocket analogy) and market risk's price swings get no picture, and the closing RBI column is partly hidden by a promo banner.

voice.notes: About 191 words per minute, friendly and direct ('aap samajhte ho', 'soch ke dekho'). Asks a question and answers it at once ('answer hai: padega, bilkul padega'). Uses everyday Hindi images and idioms: jeb kat jaayegi, taala lagna tay hai, dakaiti. Explains a term by its word root (credit = udhaar). Terms and abbreviations are spoken in English letter by letter (C.A.R., C.R.A.R.). Years are read plainly; one year (Basel 1) differs between the transcript and the screen.

game_ideas.player_does: Runs a bank for several rounds: takes deposits, lends to borrowers of different risk, invests surplus, and chooses how much to keep aside as a cushion (the 'inner pocket').
game_ideas.process_happens: Each round a shock may hit: a borrower defaults (the interest loop gets a red cross), share prices drop, or a cyber attack hits; losses come out of the cushion first.
game_ideas.win: Survive all rounds with every depositor repaid while still earning interest.
game_ideas.lose: A shock larger than the cushion stamps the FAIL seal; depositors queue at other banks too (contagion), showing why Basel asks for money kept aside.
game_ideas.concept: Basel norms: keep money aside against risk

game_ideas.player_does: Sorts bank events into credit, market or operational risk: borrower does not repay, bond prices fall, server crashes, robbery, gold price swings, fraud by staff.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each correct card lights its entry on the sidebar risk map and plays its picture (crossed loop, falling price line, broken server).
game_ideas.lose: A wrong card lights the wrong sidebar box and shows the event's real picture with its risk name.

game_ideas.player_does: Links the chain of a bank failure in order: bank fails, depositors lose savings, trust falls, runs on other banks, banks cannot lend, industry stops growing, economic downturn, world effect.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each correct link lights the next node and spreads a red tint from the first bank to others, then to factories and to a globe.
game_ideas.win: Full chain built from one bank to the world economy.
game_ideas.lose: A link out of order breaks the chain and shows the missing step (for example runs on other banks before trust falls).
game_ideas.concept: bank failure and its chain of effects

checks_learned: A spoken analogy must get a picture in the scene plan; here the strongest idea (inner-pocket cash on a bus) has none.
Content promised 'in this video' (CAR, CRAR, RWA, tier capital) must be delivered or explicitly moved to the next video before the end.
Spoken years and numbers must match on-screen text (Basel 1: transcript 1998, screen 1988); a check should compare them and flag for audio review.
Abbreviation-to-full-name lines with no idea drawn (CAR, CRAR, RWA) should be flagged as names without meaning.
A consequence chain (failure, contagion, credit crunch, downturn) must be drawn as a chain, not as bullets.
'Prices fluctuate' needs a moving price line; a list of asset names does not show market risk.
A sidebar chapter map that lights the current part worked; enforce it for overview-then-details videos.

teaching_best.why: A red FAIL seal on the bank and 'bank fail hone ka matlab?' set the stakes before any term.
A spoken cause chain from one failed bank to all banks, to industry, to the economy, to the world, closed by a question the narrator answers himself.
The bus inner-pocket analogy makes 'keep capital aside' obvious to any learner (voice only).
Credit risk as a story: interest loop, more loans more risk, deposits flowing in, the loop crossed out, FAIL seal, then filed under 'credit risk' with an etymology unpack.
BIS as a hub with two-way arrows to central banks, and BCBS as a committee table with heads: institutions as small pictures.

teaching_weak.why: The consequences of failure are four text bullets; contagion and credit crunch are never drawn.
CAR, CRAR and RWA appear only as abbreviation lines, are promised for this video, and are never explained.
BIS facts as plain text lines read aloud.
Market risk and operational risk are short lists; nothing moves or breaks.
Basel 1's year differs between the transcript and the screen, and a promo banner covers the closing RBI column.
